nameStory: The name 'smooth hawkweed' refers to its relatively hairless stems and leaves compared to its fuzzier cousins in the hawkweed family. Ancient folklore claimed that hawks would eat these plants to sharpen their eyesight, giving the entire hawkweed group its common name. The 'smooth' part helps distinguish it from the notoriously hairy mouse-eared hawkweed that feels like velvet to the touch.
description: Smooth hawkweed is a tall perennial wildflower that can tower over three feet high, making it one of the giants in the hawkweed family. It produces bright yellow daisy-like flowers arranged in loose clusters at the top of sturdy, upright stems. This European native has established itself throughout New England's disturbed areas, spreading through underground rhizomes that help it form colonies. Unlike many of its relatives, this species lives up to its 'smooth' name with relatively hairless leaves and stems.

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Tall, erect stems rising 2-4 feet high from spreading underground rhizomes, often forming patches or colonies

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow daisy-like flower heads arranged in loose, branching clusters at stem tips, each flower about 1 inch across with many narrow petals

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Variable in size and shape, relatively smooth to the touch compared to other hawkweeds, with sparse hairs rather than the dense fuzz of relatives

idTips.label: Stems
idTips.description: Sturdy, upright stems that feel relatively smooth when you run your fingers along them, lacking the dense hairiness of mouse-eared hawkweed

idTips.label: Seeds
idTips.description: Small seeds topped with fluffy white parachutes (pappus) that drift on the wind like tiny dandelion seeds

habitat: Look for smooth hawkweed in disturbed areas throughout New England, especially abandoned fields, old pastures, and roadside ditches. It thrives in sunny to partially shaded spots with average to poor soils, often establishing along lakeshores, riverbanks, and forest edges. This adaptable plant tolerates a wide range of conditions from sandy beaches to clay-rich former farmland.

seasonality.spring: New shoots emerge from underground rhizomes, with fresh leaves developing in rosettes before the tall flowering stems begin to rise.
seasonality.summer: Bright yellow flowers bloom from June through August, creating showy displays in disturbed areas and field edges.
seasonality.fall: Seeds develop fluffy white parachutes and disperse on autumn winds, while leaves may persist in mild weather.
seasonality.winter: Above-ground parts die back, but the extensive underground rhizome system survives to sprout new colonies next spring.

funFact: This plant is such an aggressive colonizer that Australia has declared all hawkweed species as prohibited weeds and runs volunteer eradication programs to hunt them down, treating them like botanical criminals on the run!
confusionNotes: Smooth hawkweed is most easily confused with other yellow hawkweeds, but its tall height and relatively hairless stems set it apart. Remember: if it feels fuzzy and stays low, it's probably mouse-eared hawkweed; if it towers above your knees and feels smooth, you've found the smooth hawkweed.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'smooth,' this hawkweed isn't completely hairless—it's just much less fuzzy than its relatives. The scientific name has changed over time, and you might see it listed as Hieracium piloselloides in older field guides, though it's now properly classified as Pilosella piloselloides.
compareHints: Smooth hawkweed towers above its mouse-eared hawkweed cousin, which stays close to the ground in creeping mats with densely fuzzy leaves. While orange hawkweed catches attention with its fiery blooms, smooth hawkweed sticks to classic yellow flowers. The key difference is height and hairiness—smooth hawkweed stands tall with relatively bare stems, while most other Pilosella species hug the ground with noticeably fuzzy textures.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Orange hawkweed stands out from its hawkweed relatives by its distinctive orange-red flowers—most other hawkweeds in New England have yellow blooms.
Mouse-eared hawkweed stands out from its hawkweed relatives by its distinctively fuzzy, silvery leaves and single yellow flowers on leafless stems.
Meadow hawkweed differs from its orange hawkweed cousin by having yellow flowers instead of orange-red ones.
Yellow-devil differs from orange hawkweed by its yellow (not orange-red) flowers and generally paler, more silvery-fuzzy leaves.
Yellow Devil differs from Orange Hawkweed by its yellow (not orange-red) flowers and more tightly clustered flower heads.
